stem: Which environment variables turn on LangSmith tracing for a LangChain app, with no code changes?

options.text: `LANGSMITH_TRACING=true` plus `LANGSMITH_API_KEY` (a project name is optional)
options.why: Correct: the flag switches tracing on, the key authenticates, and the project name is optional.

options.text: Only `LANGSMITH_PROJECT`; naming a project is enough to start sending traces
options.why: A project name alone neither enables tracing nor authenticates the upload.

options.text: `LANGSMITH_DEBUG=1`, which prints every run to the console and uploads it
options.why: That is not how tracing is enabled; console debugging and LangSmith upload are separate.

options.text: None; tracing must be enabled by passing a tracer object to every `invoke` call
options.why: LangChain picks up the environment variables automatically, so per-call tracers are optional.

explanation: Set `LANGSMITH_TRACING=true` and `LANGSMITH_API_KEY`, and optionally `LANGSMITH_PROJECT`; every LangChain and LangGraph run is then logged. Without a project name, LangSmith creates a default project on ingestion. Accounts outside the US region also set `LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT` to their regional API URL.

stem: An interviewer asks where LangSmith fits next to LangChain and LangGraph. Which statements hold? (Choose two.)

options.text: It is a platform for tracing, debugging and evaluating LLM apps
options.why: That is its role: observability plus datasets and evaluations.

options.text: It can trace code that does not use LangChain at all, for example through `@traceable`
options.why: Manual instrumentation works with any code, regardless of framework.

options.text: It is the library that provides `create_agent` and the Runnable interface
options.why: Those live in `langchain` and `langchain-core`; LangSmith observes them rather than providing them.

options.text: It only works with agents built on LangGraph
options.why: Plain LangChain chains, raw SDK calls and other frameworks can all be traced.

options.text: Installing it replaces the need for unit tests, because every run is recorded
options.why: Traces show what happened; they do not assert anything. Tests and evals are still needed.

explanation: LangChain is the framework for building, LangGraph is the low-level orchestration runtime, and LangSmith is the platform for traces, datasets, experiments and monitoring. LangSmith is framework-agnostic: `@traceable` and SDK wrappers trace any Python code. When an agent misbehaves in production, LangSmith is where you start looking.

stem: After `set_llm_cache(InMemoryCache())`, cached responses survive a process restart and are shared by every worker process of the app.

options.text: True
options.why: An in-memory cache lives in one process's memory, so it is neither persistent nor shared.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the cache is lost on restart and each process has its own copy.

explanation: `InMemoryCache` is a dictionary in the current process (optionally bounded with `maxsize`, evicting the oldest entries). For a cache that survives restarts on one machine, use `SQLiteCache` from `langchain_community.cache`; for a cache shared by many workers, use a networked backend such as Redis.

stem: Which function from `langchain_core.globals` installs a cache for every chat model call in the process? Type the function name.
explanation: `set_llm_cache(InMemoryCache())` installs a global cache, and `set_llm_cache(None)` disables it. In LangChain 1.x import it from `langchain_core.globals`; the old `langchain.globals` module no longer exists in the `langchain` package.

stem: A unit test must make the fake model return an `AIMessage` with a specific tool call on the first turn and plain text on the second. Which fake fits best?

options.text: `FakeListChatModel(responses=[...])` with the tool call written out as text
options.why: It takes plain strings and cycles through them, so it cannot script a tool call.

options.text: `GenericFakeChatModel(messages=iter([...]))`
options.why: Correct: it returns each `AIMessage` from the iterator in turn, tool calls included.

options.text: `FakeEmbeddings(size=8)`
options.why: That fakes an embedding model, not a chat model.

options.text: A real model with `temperature=0`
options.why: That still makes network calls, costs money and is not guaranteed deterministic.

explanation: `GenericFakeChatModel` takes an iterator of `AIMessage` objects (or strings) and returns one per call, so you control every turn exactly, including `tool_calls`. `FakeListChatModel` is handier for plain-text replies and cycles back to the first response when it runs out. Neither needs an API key.

stem: An old script does `from langchain.chains import LLMChain`. On `langchain` 1.x it fails with `ModuleNotFoundError`. What is the quickest way to get it running unchanged in behaviour?

options.text: Pin `langchain-core` to 0.3 and keep `langchain` 1.x
options.why: Mixing majors does not bring back the removed module and breaks dependency resolution.

options.text: Install `langchain-community`, which re-exports every legacy chain from 0.x
options.why: Legacy chains are not in `langchain-community`; they moved to `langchain-classic`.

options.text: Install `langchain-classic` and import from `langchain_classic.chains`
options.why: Correct: the legacy chains moved there unchanged.

options.text: Replace the import with `from langchain.agents import LLMChain`
options.why: `langchain.agents` holds `create_agent`, not legacy chains.

explanation: LangChain 1.x trimmed the `langchain` namespace to agents, messages, tools, chat models and embeddings. Legacy chains, retrievers, the indexing API, the hub module and other deprecated code live in `langchain-classic`. Installing it and switching imports to `langchain_classic.*` is the stop-gap; the real migration rewrites those chains with LCEL or `create_agent`.

stem: An interviewer asks why you used LangChain instead of calling a provider SDK directly. Which answer is strongest?

options.text: LangChain makes model calls faster than the provider SDK because it batches requests
options.why: It wraps the SDK, so it adds a little overhead rather than removing any.

options.text: Provider SDKs cannot call tools or return structured JSON, so a framework is required
options.why: Provider SDKs support tool calling and structured output natively.

options.text: A single interface over models, tools and retrievers, so pieces swap and compose
options.why: Correct: portability and composition are what you are buying.

options.text: LangChain is required to use LangSmith tracing
options.why: LangSmith traces non-LangChain code too, for example via `@traceable`.

explanation: The docs pitch LangChain as a standard interface for chat models, embeddings and more across providers, plus an agent harness (`create_agent` with middleware). That pays off when the app has several moving parts or may switch providers. A good answer also names the cost: an extra abstraction layer to learn and debug.

stem: `InMemoryRateLimiter(requests_per_second=2)` attached to a chat model limits how many tokens per second the app sends to the provider.

options.text: True
options.why: Its "tokens" are bucket tokens for requests, not LLM tokens; prompt size is ignored.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: it limits the number of requests over time, not their size.

explanation: The limiter is a token bucket where each request spends one bucket token. The docs warn that it only limits requests per unit of time and does not help if you must also limit by request size, such as provider tokens-per-minute quotas.

stem: Your RAG app calls a custom retriever that queries Elasticsearch with plain Python, then a LangChain chain. You want the retriever step to appear as its own span inside the same LangSmith trace. What do you do?

options.text: Decorate the retriever function with `@traceable(run_type="retriever")`
options.why: Correct: the decorated call becomes a child run of whatever trace is active.

options.text: Log the retriever's results with `print`; LangSmith captures stdout
options.why: LangSmith does not read stdout; nothing is recorded.

options.text: Rewrite the retriever as a `BaseRetriever` subclass; plain functions cannot be traced
options.why: Rewriting works but is not required; `@traceable` traces any function.

options.text: Start a second LangSmith project for non-LangChain code
options.why: A separate project splits the trace instead of nesting the span.

explanation: `@traceable` wraps any function so its inputs and outputs are logged as a run, nested under the active parent run (another traceable function or a LangChain runnable). `run_type` (`chain` by default; also `tool`, `retriever`, `llm` and others) controls how the span is shown. With tracing disabled, the decorated function just runs normally.

stem: A global cache is set with `set_llm_cache(InMemoryCache())`. One creative-writing model in the same app must always call the provider. What is the cleanest way to do that?

options.text: Call `set_llm_cache(None)` before each call to that model and restore it afterwards
options.why: That switches the cache off for every model in the process, and races with concurrent requests.

options.text: Construct that model with `cache=False`
options.why: Correct: the model then skips the global cache entirely.

options.text: Raise that model's `temperature`, which makes LangChain skip caching
options.why: Temperature does not turn caching off; a cache would freeze one sampled answer.

options.text: Nothing can be done; caching is global or off
options.why: Every chat model has a `cache` field for exactly this.

explanation: A chat model's `cache` field decides: `None` (default) uses the global cache, `False` never caches, and a `BaseCache` instance uses that cache for this model only. `cache=True` with no global cache raises `ValueError` ("Asked to cache, but no cache found"). Running it on fake models confirms each behaviour.

stem:
Which statements about this code are true? (Choose two.)

```python
from langchain_core.callbacks import get_usage_metadata_callback

with get_usage_metadata_callback() as cb:
    small_model.invoke("a")
    small_model.invoke("b")
    large_model.invoke("c")
print(cb.usage_metadata)
```

options.text: `cb.usage_metadata` is a dict keyed by model name, with token counts summed per model
options.why: Correct: both `small_model` calls are added together under one key.

options.text: It collects usage from every chat model call made inside the `with` block, without passing callbacks by hand
options.why: Correct: the context manager registers the handler for calls in its scope.

options.text: It reports the dollar cost of each call using a built-in price table
options.why: It aggregates token counts from `usage_metadata`; pricing is up to you.

options.text: It only works with OpenAI models
options.why: It reads the provider-neutral `AIMessage.usage_metadata`, so any model that reports usage works.

options.text: It returns only the usage of the last call made in the block
options.why: Usage is accumulated across all calls, not overwritten.

explanation: `get_usage_metadata_callback()` (or `UsageMetadataCallbackHandler` passed via `config={"callbacks": [...]}`) adds up each response's `usage_metadata`, keyed by the model name in the response metadata. That gives per-model totals for a request; multiply by your own price table for cost.

stem:
This test fails before the model is ever invoked. Why?

```python
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain_core.language_models import GenericFakeChatModel

model = GenericFakeChatModel(messages=iter([AIMessage("hi")]))
agent = create_agent(model, tools=[get_weather])
agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "weather?"}]})
```

options.text: `create_agent` only accepts provider strings such as `"anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5"`, not instances
options.why: It accepts model instances too; the fake works when no tools are bound.

options.text: The iterator holds one message, and the agent needs at least two
options.why: A single text reply would end the loop; that is not where it fails.

options.text: `GenericFakeChatModel` has no `bind_tools`, which `create_agent` calls when tools are given
options.why: Correct: it raises `NotImplementedError`; subclass it with a `bind_tools` that returns `self`.

options.text: Fake models cannot be used inside LangGraph graphs
options.why: They can; with a `bind_tools` stub the whole agent loop runs offline.

explanation: With tools, `create_agent` binds them to the model, and the fake raises `NotImplementedError`. The documented fix is a small subclass whose `bind_tools` returns the model unchanged; script a tool-call `AIMessage` followed by a final answer to test the full loop. Running both versions confirms the error and the fix.

stem: Match each evaluation need with the evaluator type that fits it best.

options.text: Code (heuristic) evaluator
options.why: Deterministic rule check, such as valid JSON or non-empty output.

options.text: LLM-as-judge evaluator
options.why: A model grades outputs against criteria in a prompt.

options.text: Human annotation
options.why: People review outputs or traces, often in an annotation queue.

options.text: Pairwise evaluator
options.why: Compares outputs from two versions and picks the better one.

prompts.text: Check that every answer parses as JSON matching the schema
Score helpfulness and tone on thousands of answers each night
Build a trusted gold set for a new legal domain
Decide which of two prompt versions gives better summaries

explanation: LangSmith offers code, LLM-as-judge, human and pairwise evaluators. Use cheap deterministic code checks wherever a rule exists, LLM judges for fuzzy qualities, humans to build trusted labels, and pairwise comparisons when absolute scores are noisy but preferences are clear.

stem: A chat model has `rate_limiter=InMemoryRateLimiter(requests_per_second=0.5, max_bucket_size=1)`. A fresh process makes three calls in a row from one thread, and each call itself is instant. Roughly how long do the three calls take?

options.text: About 0 seconds, because the first two calls burst through
options.why: With `max_bucket_size=1` there is no burst, and the bucket starts empty.

options.text: About 4 seconds, because the first call goes through immediately
options.why: The bucket starts with no tokens, so even the first call waits.

options.text: About 6 seconds: each call waits about 2 seconds for a token
options.why: Correct: one token every 2 seconds, and the first call waits too.

options.text: About 1.5 seconds, because the limit is per minute
options.why: `requests_per_second` is per second; 0.5 means one request every 2 seconds.

explanation: The limiter refills `requests_per_second` tokens per second up to `max_bucket_size`, and each request spends one. It starts empty, so in a fresh process the first request also waits. A timing run with `requests_per_second=2` showed calls finishing at about 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 seconds and so on. Raise `max_bucket_size` to allow bursts after idle time.

stem: Support wants to find every trace for customer `acme` in LangSmith. The app is an LCEL chain called from a FastAPI handler. What is the simplest reliable approach?

options.text: Create one LangSmith project per customer at deploy time and route traces there
options.why: Projects are per app or environment; per-customer projects do not scale and split dashboards.

options.text: Put the customer id in the prompt text so it shows up in the trace
options.why: It pollutes the prompt and costs tokens; filters work on metadata, not prompt text.

options.text: Add a custom callback that writes the customer id to a log file next to the trace id
options.why: That log is not linked to LangSmith traces, so support cannot filter by it.

options.text: Invoke with `config={"metadata": {"customer_id": "acme"}}` and filter on that key
options.why: Correct: config metadata is recorded on the run and inherited by child runs.

explanation: Tags and metadata passed through `RunnableConfig` (at invoke time or with `with_config`) are attached to the run and inherited by child runs, so you can filter and group traces by them. Outside LangChain, `@traceable(metadata=...)`, `langsmith_extra` or `tracing_context(metadata=...)` do the same. A `thread_id` metadata key groups traces into threads.

stem: Put the steps of a first offline evaluation in LangSmith in order.

options.text: Create a dataset of examples with inputs and, where possible, reference outputs
Write a target function that takes an example's inputs and runs your app
Write evaluators that score outputs, optionally against reference outputs
Call `evaluate(target, data=..., evaluators=[...])`, which records an experiment
Compare the experiment with earlier ones and inspect the low-scoring examples

explanation: A dataset holds examples; the target receives only each example's `inputs`; evaluators receive the inputs, the actual outputs and the reference outputs. Each `evaluate()` call produces an experiment, and comparing experiments over the same dataset is how you tell whether a change helped.

stem:
Each `small` reply reports 100 input and 10 output tokens; each `large` reply reports 400 input and 50 output tokens. What does the last line print? Type a number.

```python
with get_usage_metadata_callback() as cb:
    small.invoke("a")
    small.invoke("b")
    large.invoke("c")
print(cb.usage_metadata["small"]["total_tokens"])
```
explanation: Usage is summed per model name: two `small` calls of 110 tokens each give 220. The `large` call is recorded under its own key (450). Running this with `GenericFakeChatModel` replies that carry `usage_metadata` and a `model_name` prints 220.

stem: Which project is the weakest case for adding LangChain?

options.text: A support agent that calls six internal tools and needs human approval for refunds
options.why: Tool calling, middleware and interrupts are exactly what the agent harness provides.

options.text: A nightly script that sends one fixed prompt to one provider and saves the text
options.why: Correct: one call with no tools, retrieval or steps gains little from a framework.

options.text: A RAG service that must be able to swap its embedding model and vector store
options.why: Uniform interfaces for embeddings and vector stores make that swap cheaper.

options.text: A product that must run against two model providers with the same code
options.why: A provider-neutral chat model interface is one of the main reasons to use it.

explanation: Frameworks pay off when there are several moving parts: tools, retrieval, multi-step flows, provider switching, tracing. A single prompt to a single provider is simpler and easier to debug with the provider SDK, and can still be traced with `@traceable`.

stem: You publish a LangChain integration for a new chat model and adopt the `langchain-tests` standard tests. How are the two suites split?

options.text: Unit tests run without the service; integration tests call the real service
options.why: Correct: that is the documented split, in `tests/unit_tests` and `tests/integration_tests`.

options.text: Unit tests call the real API once to record it; integration tests replay the recordings
options.why: It is the other way round: unit tests never touch the network.

options.text: Both suites call the real API, but integration tests also check streaming
options.why: The unit suite is designed to run without access to external services.

options.text: There is only one suite, and every test runs for every model
options.why: Most standard tests are opt-in through capability properties and are skipped otherwise.

explanation: `langchain-tests` provides pytest suites per integration type: `langchain_tests.unit_tests` for isolated checks and `langchain_tests.integration_tests` for checks against the live service. You subclass the suite and override capability properties (for example image input support) so unsupported features are skipped. Pin the package version, because new releases can add tests that break CI.

stem: A customer reports at 3am that the production agent gave a confidently wrong refund amount. Tracing is on. What is the best first step?

options.text: Re-run the same question locally against your laptop's setup
options.why: Local runs may not reproduce production state, data or model versions.

options.text: Raise the model's `max_retries` and redeploy
options.why: Retries do not fix a wrong answer, and you do not yet know the cause.

options.text: Open that request's trace and inspect each model and tool step
options.why: Correct: the trace shows where the wrong number first appeared.

options.text: Switch to a larger model, since wrong answers usually mean the model is too small
options.why: Guessing at the cause before reading the trace often misses tool or data bugs.

explanation: Find the failing trace (filter by user, thread or metadata), then walk the runs: was the right tool called with the right arguments, did the tool return the right data, did the prompt contain it, and where did the wrong value first appear? Then add the case to a dataset so the fix can be regression-tested.

stem: Which statements about LangSmith offline evaluation are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Reference outputs in a dataset are given to evaluators, not to the application under test
options.why: Correct: the target receives only the example's inputs.

options.text: Each `evaluate()` run over a dataset is recorded as an experiment you can compare with others
options.why: Correct: experiments are how versions are compared on the same examples.

options.text: Every example must have a reference output, or `evaluate()` refuses to run
options.why: Reference outputs are optional; reference-free evaluators need only the outputs.

options.text: Offline evaluation scores live production runs as they arrive
options.why: That is online evaluation; offline runs on curated datasets before deployment.

options.text: Evaluators must be LLM-as-judge prompts; plain Python functions are not supported
options.why: Plain functions returning a bool or score are the simplest evaluators.

explanation: Offline evaluation runs a version of the app over a dataset before release: benchmarking, regression testing, backtesting. Examples hold inputs, optional reference outputs and metadata. Gate releases by comparing a candidate's experiment with the current baseline on the same dataset.

stem: Which evaluator correctly scores exact matches in `langsmith.evaluate(target, data="qa-set", evaluators=[...])`, where the target and each example's outputs both look like `{"answer": ...}`?

options.text: `def check(run_output, expected_output): return run_output == expected_output`
options.why: With two unrecognised names the SDK assumes the legacy `(run, example)` form, so this compares a run object with an `Example` and never matches.

options.text: `def check(example): return example["answer"] == "42"`
options.why: An `Example` holds `inputs` and `outputs`; and this never looks at the app's output.

options.text: `def check(outputs, reference_outputs): return outputs == reference_outputs`
options.why: Correct: the SDK fills these arguments by name and records the bool as a score; equal dicts mean a match.

options.text: `def check(inputs): return len(inputs) > 0`
options.why: It runs but only inspects the inputs, so it measures nothing about the app.

explanation: The SDK fills evaluator arguments by name from `run`, `example`, `inputs`, `outputs`, `reference_outputs` and `attachments`. Returning a bool records a score under the function's name. A function with exactly two unrecognised parameter names is treated as the legacy `(run, example)` signature, which silently breaks a naive comparison. Local runs with `upload_results=False` confirmed both behaviours.

stem: You evaluate an agent's tool-call trajectory against a reference with `agentevals`' trajectory match evaluator. Match each requirement with the `trajectory_match_mode` that enforces it.

options.text: `strict`
options.why: Same message structure and tool calls in the same order.

options.text: `unordered`
options.why: Same tool calls as the reference, in any order.

options.text: `subset`
options.why: Only tools from the reference may be called; no extras.

options.text: `superset`
options.why: At least the reference tools; extra calls are allowed.

prompts.text: Compliance flow: always verify identity, then look up the account, then refund
Weather and time lookups are both required, but may run in either order
The agent must never call any tool outside the approved list for this task
The agent must call the search tool, and may also call other tools

explanation: Final-answer checks miss an agent that reaches the right answer by the wrong route. Trajectory evaluators compare the tool calls: `strict` for ordered workflows, `unordered` when order does not matter, `subset` to forbid extra (possibly costly or risky) tools, `superset` to require certain tools while allowing exploration. By default, tool calls match only if their arguments match too; `tool_args_match_mode` relaxes that.

stem: Gunicorn runs your API with 8 worker processes on one machine. Each process builds its model with `rate_limiter=InMemoryRateLimiter(requests_per_second=5)`. The provider allows 10 requests per second for your key. What happens at peak?

options.text: The app stays at 5 requests per second, because the limiter is thread safe
options.why: Thread safety covers threads within one process; each worker has its own bucket.

options.text: Up to about 40 per second, so 429s continue; use a shared limiter or gateway
options.why: Correct: 8 independent buckets of 5 each.

options.text: Exactly 10 per second, because the limiter reads the provider's rate-limit headers
options.why: It knows nothing about the provider; it only counts its own requests.

options.text: About 5 per second in total, because the processes share the bucket through the OS
options.why: In-memory state is not shared between processes.

explanation: `InMemoryRateLimiter` is thread safe and works in sync or async code, but it is not designed to coordinate across processes or machines. Divide the budget per process, or put a shared limiter (for example in Redis or an API gateway) in front. Keep `max_retries` with backoff as the safety net for the 429s that still happen.

stem: Put a safe migration of a large 0.x codebase (with `LLMChain`, `RetrievalQA` and `AgentExecutor`) to LangChain 1.x in order.

options.text: Add tests or a small eval dataset that captures today's behaviour
Upgrade to Python 3.10+ and `langchain` 1.x, and install `langchain-classic`
Point legacy imports at `langchain_classic.*` and confirm the tests still pass
Rewrite the chains as LCEL and the agent with `create_agent`, one piece at a time
Remove the `langchain-classic` dependency once nothing imports it

explanation: Capture behaviour first, so each later step can be checked. LangChain 1.x needs Python 3.10+. `langchain-classic` gets the old code running on the new packages with only import changes. Then replace legacy pieces incrementally (LCEL for fixed pipelines, `create_agent` for agents), and drop the compatibility package last.

stem: A bank's FAQ bot adds a semantic cache (`score_threshold` loosened to raise the hit rate). Soon "How do I close my savings account?" is answered with the cached reply to "How do I open a savings account?". What is the best fix?

options.text: Switch to `InMemoryCache`, which also matches similar prompts but more conservatively
options.why: `InMemoryCache` is exact-match only; it would stop the wrong hits but also most hits.

options.text: Use a larger chat model so the cached answer is better
options.why: The model is never called on a hit, so its size is irrelevant.

options.text: Tighten the threshold, test it on near-miss pairs, and skip intent-critical queries
options.why: Correct: the threshold decides what counts as the same question.

options.text: Add a TTL so cached entries expire after an hour and stale answers age out quickly
options.why: Expiry limits stale answers but still serves wrong ones within the hour.

explanation: An exact-match cache keys on the serialized prompt plus the model's parameters, so it only hits on identical calls. A semantic cache embeds the prompt and returns a stored answer within a similarity threshold, which raises hit rates but can return the answer to a different question that looks similar, such as open versus close. Tune the threshold on labelled near-miss pairs, and scope or disable it where one word changes the meaning.

stem: An agent calls a model, then a `charge_card` tool, then the model again. Which retry and timeout practices are sound? (Choose two.)

options.text: Retry 429 and 5xx responses with exponential backoff and jitter, but not 400, 401 or 404
options.why: Correct: transient errors may succeed later; client errors will fail the same way again.

options.text: Only retry `charge_card` if it is idempotent, for example with an idempotency key
options.why: Correct: a retry after a timeout may repeat a charge that actually succeeded.

options.text: Set no timeout on model calls, so slow responses are never wasted
options.why: A hung call then holds the request forever; timeouts plus retries bound the latency.

options.text: Retry the whole agent run from the start whenever any step fails
options.why: That repeats tool side effects and multiplies cost; retry the failing step.

options.text: Use the same large retry count at every layer: SDK, model wrapper and agent
options.why: Nested retries multiply: 6 at each of three layers can mean hundreds of attempts.

explanation: Retry transient errors (network, 429, 5xx) with backoff and jitter; LangChain chat models do this by default (`max_retries` 6) and do not retry client errors such as 401 or 404. Side-effecting tools need idempotency before they are retried. Set timeouts per call and an overall deadline, and keep retries at one layer so they do not multiply.

stem: Your service handles 2 million agent requests a day, and tracing every one is too costly. You want about 10% of requests in LangSmith, each with its full tree of child runs. What do you set?

options.text: `LANGSMITH_TRACING=0.1`
options.why: That variable is an on or off flag, not a rate.

options.text: Tag 10% of calls with `sample=true`; LangSmith drops untagged runs
options.why: LangSmith does not drop runs by tag; untagged runs would still be stored.

options.text: Set `max_concurrency=10` in the config
options.why: That limits parallelism in `batch`; it has nothing to do with tracing.

options.text: `LANGSMITH_TRACING_SAMPLING_RATE=0.1`
options.why: Correct: a float from 0 to 1 that samples traces.

explanation: `LANGSMITH_TRACING_SAMPLING_RATE` takes a float from 0 (no traces) to 1 (all traces; the default). Sampling is decided per trace, so a sampled request keeps its full run tree. You can also give a `Client(tracing_sampling_rate=...)` to `tracing_context` for different rates per code path, for example 100% for errors in a canary.

stem: A user gives a thumbs-down on a wrong answer in production. Put the steps that turn it into a regression test in order.

options.text: Record the feedback on the run with `client.create_feedback(...)`
Filter traces by that feedback and inspect the failing trace
Add the run's inputs to a dataset with a corrected reference output
Run the candidate fix as an experiment over that dataset
Release only if the new experiment beats the baseline without regressions

explanation: Feedback attaches a score to a run, so bad answers become filterable. Adding the input to a dataset with a corrected reference turns one complaint into a permanent test case, and every future change is gated on an experiment over that dataset. Online evaluators can flag such runs automatically, but they usually have no reference output, which is why the corrected answer is added by hand.

stem: You must test that an agent remembers a user's city from turn 1 when answering turn 2, without network calls. Which setup does this?

options.text: A fake model scripted for both turns, `create_agent(..., checkpointer=InMemorySaver())`, and the same `thread_id` for both invokes
options.why: Correct: the checkpointer restores turn 1's messages on turn 2.

options.text: A real model at `temperature=0` with a VCR cassette, and a new `thread_id` per turn
options.why: A new thread starts with empty state, so turn 2 cannot see turn 1.

options.text: A fake model and no checkpointer, passing only the new message on turn 2
options.why: Without a checkpointer nothing persists between invocations.

options.text: An LLM-as-judge eval over production traces
options.why: That is evaluation, not a deterministic offline test of the memory wiring.

explanation: Unit tests use in-memory fakes: a scripted chat model plus `InMemorySaver` to simulate several turns. In a run with a fake model, the second invoke on the same thread saw 6 messages (4 from turn 1 plus the new pair). Keep fixtures function-scoped, because a shared iterator runs out and breaks later tests.

stem: On `langchain` 1.4, match each name with the module you import it from.

options.text: `langchain_classic.chains`
options.why: Legacy chain classes.

options.text: `langchain_community.cache`
options.why: Community cache backends.

options.text: `langchain_core.globals`
options.why: Process-wide settings such as the global cache.

options.text: `langchain_core.rate_limiters`
options.why: Core request rate limiters.

explanation: LangChain 1.x moved legacy chains into `langchain-classic`; third-party cache backends such as `SQLiteCache` and `RedisSemanticCache` live in `langchain-community`; `set_llm_cache` is in `langchain_core.globals` (there is no `langchain.globals` any more); `InMemoryRateLimiter` is in `langchain_core.rate_limiters`. Each import was checked in a fresh environment.

stem: When a chat model has both a cache and a `rate_limiter`, a cache hit returns without consuming a rate-limiter token.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: the model checks the cache first and only acquires a token before a real call.

options.text: False
options.why: In `langchain-core` the rate limiter is acquired after the cache lookup, so hits skip it.

explanation: Inside the chat model, the cache lookup comes first, and the limiter is acquired only when the provider will actually be called. A timing run confirmed it: with `requests_per_second=1`, four identical calls took about 1 second in total (one real call that waited for a token, then three instant hits).

stem:
How many times does the fake model actually generate a reply (that is, miss the cache)? Type a number.

```python
set_llm_cache(InMemoryCache())
model = FakeListChatModel(responses=["r1", "r2", "r3", "r4"])

model.invoke("hi")
model.invoke("hi")
model.invoke("Hi")
model.invoke("hi", stop=["\n"])
model.invoke("hi")
```
explanation: The cache key is the serialized prompt plus a string of the model's parameters and call options. Calls 1, 3 and 4 miss: `"Hi"` is a different prompt, and `stop` changes the parameter string. Calls 2 and 5 repeat call 1 exactly and hit. Running it returns `r1, r1, r2, r3, r1`, so the model generated 3 times.

stem: Your LLM-as-judge for "answer is grounded in the context" will gate releases. How do you check it can be trusted?

options.text: Use the strongest available model as the judge; stronger judges need no checking
options.why: Even strong judges have biases and blind spots on your domain; agreement must be measured.

options.text: Run the judge twice and accept it if it agrees with itself
options.why: Self-consistency shows stability, not correctness; it can be consistently wrong.

options.text: Have humans label a sample, measure agreement, and refine with corrections
options.why: Correct: human labels are the ground truth the judge is calibrated against.

options.text: Ask the judge to explain each score; if the reasoning reads well, the score is right
options.why: Fluent reasoning can rationalise a wrong score.

explanation: Treat the judge as a model to be evaluated. Label a representative sample by hand, measure agreement, and look at the disagreements. LangSmith lets you correct judge scores and feed the corrections back as few-shot examples. Re-check agreement whenever the judge model or prompt changes.

stem: A pairwise LLM judge compares answers from prompt A and prompt B. Which are known biases you should control for? (Choose two.)

options.text: Position bias: preferring whichever answer is shown first (or second)
options.why: Correct: swap the order and count a win only if it holds both ways.

options.text: Verbosity bias: preferring the longer answer even when it is not better
options.why: Correct: control for length or grade with a rubric that penalises padding.

options.text: Judges cannot compare two answers, only score one
options.why: Pairwise comparison is a standard evaluator type.

options.text: Judges always prefer answers from a different model family
options.why: The reported tendency is the opposite: self-enhancement, favouring their own style.

options.text: Judges only work when the answer contains a reference output
options.why: Many judges are reference-free, which is why they suit online evaluation.

explanation: Research on LLM judges (for example the MT-Bench study) documents position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, alongside limited reasoning on hard items. Standard mitigations: randomise or swap answer order, use explicit rubrics, prefer a judge from a different family than the models under test, and calibrate against human labels.

stem: Offline experiments show 92% correctness, but online LLM-as-judge scores in production have dropped to 70%. What is the most likely explanation and response?

options.text: The online evaluator is broken, because it has no reference outputs; trust the offline number
options.why: Reference-free scores can be noisy, but the gap is a signal to investigate, not to dismiss.

options.text: Traffic has drifted from the dataset; add low-scoring production runs as examples and re-run
options.why: Correct: the dataset no longer represents real usage.

options.text: Offline evaluations should be removed, since only production scores matter
options.why: Without offline evals you cannot test a fix before shipping it.

options.text: Raise the online sampling rate to 100%; more samples will bring the score back to 92%
options.why: Sampling more measures the drop more precisely; it does not change it.

explanation: Offline evals run on curated datasets before release; online evals score live runs, which have no reference outputs, so they use reference-free checks. When the two disagree, the dataset usually under-represents real traffic (new intents, longer inputs, other languages). Close the loop: mine failing production runs into the dataset, then gate releases on it.

stem: An internal FAQ agent is too slow and costly. Logs show 40% of requests are byte-identical repeats within a day, most of the rest are simple lookups, and answers must not change in wording for repeated questions. Which plan meets every constraint?

options.text: Add a semantic cache with a loose threshold for everything
options.why: Loose semantic matching can return the answer to a different question.

options.text: Lower `max_tokens` on every call so replies are shorter
options.why: That trims cost slightly but can truncate answers and does nothing for repeats.

options.text: Move every request to the smallest model
options.why: Hard questions would get worse answers; routing should depend on difficulty.

options.text: An exact-match response cache for repeats, plus routing easy requests to a cheaper model
options.why: Correct: repeats cost nothing and keep their wording; easy traffic gets cheaper.

explanation: Pick levers by evidence from traces and token tracking. Exact repeats are what an exact-match cache is for: zero model cost and identical wording. Routing easy requests to a cheaper model (in an agent, for example with `wrap_model_call` middleware) cuts the rest. Check both against an eval dataset so cost savings do not hide quality loss.

stem: Users say the agent feels slow: the first token arrives after 6 seconds, and the trace shows a long system prompt plus three sequential tool calls that do not depend on each other. Which changes reduce latency without lowering answer quality? (Choose three.)

options.text: Stream the final answer so users see tokens as they are generated
options.why: Correct: time to first visible token drops even if total time does not.

options.text: Let the independent tool calls run in parallel instead of one after another
options.why: Correct: three sequential waits become one.

options.text: Keep the long, stable system prompt at the start so provider prompt caching can apply
options.why: Correct: cached prefixes cut input processing time and cost on providers that support it.

options.text: Raise `max_retries` so slow calls are retried sooner
options.why: Retries handle failures, not slowness; they add load and latency.

options.text: Switch every request to the smallest model regardless of difficulty
options.why: That may be faster but lowers quality on hard requests, which breaks the constraint.

explanation: Latency work starts with the trace: where is the time going? Streaming improves perceived latency, parallel independent tool calls cut wall-clock time, and a stable prompt prefix lets provider prompt caching kick in (often only above a minimum token count). Changing models is a quality trade-off and should be checked with evals first.

stem: System design: trace ingestion for many customers at high volume, plus asynchronous LLM-graded evaluations on a sample of traces. Which design choice matters most?

options.text: Grade each trace synchronously in the ingest request, so scores are ready at once
options.why: A slow or rate-limited judge would then throttle or drop ingestion.

options.text: Store every customer's traces in one shared table with no tenant key, to keep queries simple
options.why: That makes per-customer isolation, quotas and deletion hard to enforce.

options.text: Put a queue between ingest and grading; grade sampled traces under per-tenant spend limits
options.why: Correct: ingestion stays fast and judge cost stays bounded.

options.text: Run the judge on every trace, since sampling makes scores unreliable
options.why: Judging everything multiplies cost; sampled scores with enough volume are statistically useful.

explanation: Ingestion must be fast and reliable; LLM grading is slow, costly and rate-limited. A queue between them lets each scale separately, with retries for the graders. LangSmith's own online evaluators show the same controls: filters, a sampling rate, and a per-evaluator spend limit that pauses the evaluator when hit.

stem: In a design discussion about LangChain's history, which statement accurately describes what the 1.0 release did to the `langchain` package?

options.text: It narrowed the package to agents, messages, tools, chat models and embeddings, and moved legacy chains and retrievers to `langchain-classic`
options.why: Correct: that is the 1.x namespace reduction.

options.text: It removed LCEL and Runnables in favour of LangGraph
options.why: Runnables remain in `langchain-core`; LangGraph builds on them.

options.text: It merged `langchain-core` into `langchain`, so provider packages depend on `langchain` directly
options.why: `langchain-core` remains the base package that provider integrations depend on.

options.text: It deleted the legacy chains with no compatibility path
options.why: `langchain-classic` keeps them importable while you migrate.

explanation: LangChain 1.x answers years of criticism about sprawl: `langchain` now centres on `create_agent` with middleware, a small set of standard interfaces, and LangGraph as the runtime. Legacy chains, retrievers, the indexing API, hub and community re-exports moved to `langchain-classic`. In an API-design discussion, this is the concrete example of trimming abstractions.

stem: A senior candidate is asked about the common criticism that LangChain adds abstraction overhead and hard-to-read stack traces. Which answer would impress most?

options.text: The criticism is outdated since 1.0, so there is no longer any good reason to write plain SDK code
options.why: Dismissing a valid concern is a red flag in these rounds.

options.text: Agree that frameworks are always a mistake, and build every agent by hand
options.why: That ignores what the framework does give: provider portability, middleware, persistence, tracing.

options.text: Use LangChain only for prototypes, then rewrite everything for production
options.why: A blanket rule; many teams run LangChain in production successfully.

options.text: Weigh it per project: SDK code for simple flows, the framework where it pays off, plus tracing
options.why: Correct: a balanced, evidence-based answer.

explanation: Interviewers want judgement, not loyalty. Valid criticisms: extra layers, past API churn, opaque errors. Counterpoints: 1.x trimmed the surface, `create_agent` is a thin harness, and LangSmith traces make the layers visible. Choose per project, and be able to say where you would drop down to the SDK.

stem: The primary provider has outages, so requests fail over to a second provider's model. Months later you discover answers on the fallback path were worse for weeks, and nobody noticed. What would have caught this?

options.text: Raise `max_retries` on the primary so the fallback is rarely used
options.why: It hides outages a little longer but does not measure the fallback's quality.

options.text: Tag or add metadata on fallback runs, monitor how often it is used, and run evals and online evaluators on both paths
options.why: Correct: the fallback is a second product path and needs its own quality signal.

options.text: Use the same prompt for both providers so quality is identical
options.why: A prompt tuned for one model often behaves differently on another; same prompt does not mean same quality.

options.text: Fall back only on 401 errors, which signal provider outages
options.why: 401 is an authentication error; outages show up as timeouts, 429s or 5xx.

explanation: Fallbacks protect availability, but the fallback model has different strengths, prompt sensitivities and tool-calling behaviour. Treat it as a separate path: mark its runs, alert on the fallback rate, and include it in offline experiments and online evaluation. Fall back on transient errors (timeouts, 429, 5xx), not on client errors.

stem: Design CI for a LangChain agent so it stays fast, cheap and not flaky. Which practices belong in it? (Choose three.)

options.text: Run unit tests with fake chat models and `InMemorySaver` on every commit
options.why: Correct: fast, free and deterministic.

options.text: Mark integration tests (for example `@pytest.mark.integration`) and run them before deploys, with recorded HTTP cassettes
options.why: Correct: real-API checks without paying on every run.

options.text: Assert on structure, such as tool names, argument shapes and message counts, rather than exact wording
options.why: Correct: wording varies run to run; structure is stable.

options.text: Set `temperature=0` and snapshot the exact reply text in every test
options.why: Even at temperature 0 outputs can change; exact snapshots go flaky.

options.text: Call the production model in every unit test, so tests match reality
options.why: That makes unit tests slow, costly and network-dependent.

explanation: The LangChain testing guide splits tests into unit tests (in-memory fakes), integration tests (real APIs, kept separate with a marker, using cassettes via `pytest-recording` to replay HTTP) and evals. Integration assertions should check structure, and cassettes must be re-recorded when prompts or tools change.

stem: A dashboard sums `get_usage_metadata_callback()` totals per request, and the global `InMemoryCache` serves many repeats. Finance says the dashboard shows more tokens than the provider bills. Why?

options.text: The callback double-counts streamed chunks
options.why: These calls are not streamed, and chunk usage is merged before reporting.

options.text: The provider bills only output tokens
options.why: Providers bill input tokens too.

options.text: `InMemoryCache` stores each reply twice
options.why: The cache stores one entry per prompt and parameter string; storage is not the issue.

options.text: Cache hits replay the stored reply's `usage_metadata`, so the callback counts tokens no API call used
options.why: Correct: a hit adds the original token counts again.

explanation: On a cache hit, LangChain returns the stored `AIMessage`, including its `usage_metadata` (with `total_cost` set to 0), and usage callbacks add those tokens again. A run with one real call and one hit reported twice the input tokens. For billing, count only calls that reached the provider, or use the provider's usage reports.

stem: An agent runs in AWS Lambda with LangSmith tracing on. Invocations succeed, but many traces never appear or are missing their final runs. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: Lambda blocks outbound HTTPS; open port 443
options.why: Some traces do arrive, so the network path works.

options.text: Traces are sent in the background and the function freezes first; set `LANGCHAIN_CALLBACKS_BACKGROUND=false` or call `wait_for_all_tracers()` before returning
options.why: Correct: flush tracing before the function ends.

options.text: The sampling rate defaults to 0.5 in serverless environments
options.why: All traces are logged by default; there is no serverless-specific rate.

options.text: Each Lambda needs its own `LANGSMITH_PROJECT`
options.why: Project names do not affect whether runs are delivered.

explanation: LangChain sends trace data in background threads to keep latency low. In serverless, the runtime can freeze or end once the handler returns, before those uploads finish. The docs recommend `LANGCHAIN_CALLBACKS_BACKGROUND=false` there, or `wait_for_all_tracers()` (Python) / `awaitAllCallbacks()` (JS) before exiting.
